description.text: Cybele, originally an Anatolian mother goddess, was first worshipped in Phrygia where she was associated with mountains, lions, and a black meteoric stone that served as her sacred image. The Phrygian cult spread to Greek colonies in the sixth century BC, where the Greeks adapted her as a foreign mystery‑goddess who arrived in a lion‑drawn chariot and was linked to the earth‑goddess Gaia, Rhea, and Demeter.

In Rome she was adopted as the Magna Mater during the Second Punic War, after a Sibylline oracle recommended her conscription. The Roman state built a temple on the Palatine Hill, celebrated her with the Megalesia festival, and incorporated a unique priesthood of eunuch mendicants called the Galli. The cult spread throughout the empire, and her image was made from the same meteoric stone that had been brought from Pessinus.

curiosities.text: The cult of Magna Mater included a unique priesthood of eunuch mendicants known as the Galli, who were required to castrate themselves as part of their initiation.
The statue of the goddess that was brought to Rome was made from a black meteoric stone from Pessinus, which served as the face of the statue.
